title: How much reaches the programme
question: Of every dollar an organization spends, how much does its own return put under programmes, how much under management and how much under fundraising, and where is that split out of line or arithmetically wrong?
finding: At the middle organization among 457 with $250,000 or more of spending, 82% of spending is reported as programme and 13% as management. 25 report a management share of 30% or more that is also at least twice the middle figure for their peers, led by Phatt Chance Community Services Inc at 96% against 13%. At 21 the management share rose by seven percentage points or more while City money rose by a quarter or more. 1 organization spending $1 million or more reports no management cost at all. On 5 returns the three columns do not add up to the total on the same page, or are left empty; the largest miss is $1.3 million at Southwest Community Corp.
how: From the statement of functional expenses on each full return (Part IX line 25): total expenses and its three columns. Shares are each column divided by the total. Peers are the organizations whose largest City funder over fiscal 2019 to 2026 is the same department, where there are at least eight of them; otherwise all organizations. "Far above" is a management share of 30% or more and at least twice the peer middle figure, on the latest return (returns for years ending before 2023 are too old to count as latest). "Rose" compares the first return with $100,000 or more of City money against the latest, at least two years apart. "Do not add up" is a difference of $1,000 and half of one percent in any year; a charity (section 501(c)(3)) that fills in none of the three columns is listed as leaving them empty, and such returns are kept out of the shares. Rows are ordered: arithmetic misses, then far above peers, then rose with City money, then no management cost. The largest City funder is the department that paid the organization most in the Controller's nonprofit-spending table, which counts contracted services. A rise in City money is counted only where the test is met on both of the Controller's tables, the nonprofit-spending table and the table of every payment, because where the two part it is not always established which is right.
limits: The split between programme and management is an allocation the organization makes itself, and practice varies: one body counts its site managers and rent as programme, another does not. A high management share can mean honest reporting; a share of zero can mean a parent body carries the overhead. Small and new organizations run higher. An organization that mainly passes money to others shows a very high programme share for that reason alone. Columns that do not add up are nearly always a preparer's slip. City money is taken from the Controller's table of every payment, not from its narrower nonprofit-spending table, which keeps contracted services only. Left out of it, each picked out by the payment file's own label, are: loans; money the City collects for a benefit district and hands over (the district's own assessments); benefit-plan payments from a trust fund; and debt service. For 23 of the 485 organizations matched here that makes the City figure at least $1 million and 10% higher over fiscal 2019 to 2026, $1.36 billion higher in all. The figure keeps grants and contracts the nonprofit-spending table lacks, emergency purchases, and aid paid through an organization (day care assistance, rent assistance paid on behalf of clients, in-home care contract payments). Part of that aid passes on to others, so it is a real City payment but not all of it is payment for the organization's own work. A return may not count money that passes through as revenue. For the organizations matched here, that leaves out $78.8 million of loans (9 organizations), $425.1 million of money the City collected for a benefit district and handed over (14 organizations) and $495.1 million of benefit-plan payments from a trust fund (1 organization), fiscal 2019 to 2026. District assessments are covered on the screen “Benefit districts: assessments in, City grants on top”, which keeps assessments and City grants apart. The fiscal year is the one printed on each payment, which can be later than the year the payment was made. 5 organizations met the test of a rise in City money on one table only (4 on the table of every payment, 1 on the nonprofit-spending table) and are not listed for it. A pattern here is a reason to ask for the audited statements, not a finding.
